quote_orig: ὑποστρέφοντι δὲ τῷ βασιλεῖ τούτῳ ἐκ τῆς Περσίδος τροπαιοφόρῳ πρόσεισι Μωάμεθ ὁ τῶν Σαρακηνῶν φύλαρχος, οὐκ ἐκ γένους τὸ φυλαρχεῖν κληρωσάμενος, τῶν γὰρ ἀσήμων ἐτύγχανεν ὤν, ἀλλὰ πονηρία τοῦτο κτησάμενος. πένης γὰρ ὢν παρά τινι γυναικὶ πλουσίᾳ χήρᾳ ἐθήτευεν, ἣν ἔγημε, γοητείαις ὑπαγαγὼν εἰς ἔρωτα ἑαυτοῦ. ἐπιληψίας δὲ νοσήματι συνεχόμενος, καὶ κατὰ καιροὺς αὐτῷ τοῦ πάθους προσβάλλοντος πίπτων καὶ τῶν φρενῶν ἐξιστάμενος, ἀθυμίας αἴτιος τῇ ἑαυτοῦ κυρίᾳ καὶ γαμετῇ καὶ αἰσχύνης ἐγίνετο. ὁ δὲ αὐτός τε πονηρὸς ὢν καί τινι δὲ μοναχῷ πονηροτέρῳ ἑαυτοῦ ἐντετυχηκὼς διὰ κακοπιστίαν φυγαδευθέντι τῆς Βυζαντίδος, καὶ παρ' αὐτοῦ διδαχθείς, ἔλεγε τῇ γυναικὶ τὸν Γαβριὴλ τὸν ἀρχάγγελον οὐρανόθεν αὐτῷ φοιτῶντα θεῖα τινα μυεῖν καὶ ἀπόρρητα, μὴ φέρειν δὲ τὴν τούτου θέαν καὶ διὰ τοῦτο ἰλιγγιᾶν καὶ φόβῳ συνέχεσθαι καὶ πρὸς γῆν κατακλίνεσθαι. ταῦτα δ' εἶχεν αὐτῷ συμμαρτυροῦντα καὶ τὸν μοναχὸν ἐκεῖνον τὸν δόλιον καὶ τῇ γυναικὶ λέγοντα ὅτι ὡς ἀληθῶς πᾶσι τοῖς προφήταις οὗτος ὁ Γαβριὴλ ἐπιπέμπεται. ἐντεῦθεν ἡ γυνὴ ἀποσκευαζομένη τὸ ὄνειδος, ἐγκαυχωμένη δὲ μᾶλλον ὡς συνοικοῦσα προφήτῃ, τὸν λόγον τοῦτον εἰς τὰς λοιπὰς γυναῖκας προήνεγκε, καὶ οὕτως ὄνομα προφήτου παρὰ τοῖς ὁμοφύλοις ὁ μυσαρὸς ἐκεῖνος ἐκτήσατο.
own_translation_en: Now as this emperor was returning in triumph from Persia, there came to him Muhammad, the chief of the Saracens, who had not obtained the leadership by descent, since he was one of the obscure men, but had acquired it through wickedness. Being a poor man, he served in the household of a rich widow, whom he married, having led her into love for himself by enchantments. Afflicted with the disease of epilepsy, and falling down when the attack came upon him and being out of his mind, he was a cause of despondency and shame to his wife and mistress. This wicked man, having met with a monk, even more wicked than himself, who had been exiled from Byzantium for bad faith, and having been taught by him, told his wife that the archangel Gabriel, who came to him from heaven, was initiating him into divine and secret things, and that he could not bear the sight of him, and because of this became dizzy, was seized with fear and fell to the ground. Along with these things he had the monk, that deceiver, bearing witness to him and saying to the wife that this Gabriel was truly sent to all the prophets. Thereupon the woman, to escape the disgrace, but boasting rather that she lived with a prophet, spread this story to the other women, and so that filthy man acquired the name of prophet among his own people.
licence_note: Public domain: Bonn Corpus Scriptorum Historiae Byzantinae, Zonaras vol. III (Dindorf, 1868); the item on archive.org carries no rights statement; a Bonn edition from 1868 is out of copyright. Read as page images, not only OCR.
keys: πρόσεισι Μωάμεθ ὁ τῶν Σαρακηνῶν φύλαρχος
ἔλεγε τῇ γυναικὶ τὸν Γαβριὴλ τὸν ἀρχάγγελον
ὄνομα προφήτου παρὰ τοῖς ὁμοφύλοις ὁ μυσαρὸς ἐκεῖνος ἐκτήσατο
what_it_says: Zonaras narrates Muhammad's origin in the court of Heraclius: a poor man who rose by wickedness, epileptic, who claimed that Gabriel dictated secret revelations after learning this from an exiled monk; his wife spread the claim and he gained the name of prophet.
context: Book XIV, ch. 17 of Zonaras' Epitome of Histories (Dindorf, CSHB 1868, p. 311), written in the first half of the 12th century, in the account of the Monothelete controversy and Heraclius' return from Persia. The passage is a continuous narrative, not a dialogue or a refutation. Zonaras does not name the monk.
limits: Historical-biographical polemic, not a doctrinal refutation: Zonaras discusses no Qur'anic text or Islamic dogma here, and the story is an inherited Byzantine account of Muhammad's origin (Zonaras is an epitomator; I did not trace his sources in this pass). The monk is unnamed. The word 'μυσαρός' is an insult directed at Muhammad, but the passage's point is his origin and claim to prophecy. Translation is my own literal English (no public-domain English version found).
stance: reporting (Zonaras reports the Byzantine tradition about Muhammad in his own voice; no opponent is quoted)
authenticity_note: Authentic text of Zonaras' Epitome, book XIV ch. 17 (genuine work; the story is an inherited tradition, not Zonaras' own discovery).

own_translation_en: When that woman died, he became her heir, and was called chief, teacher and lawgiver of the nation of the Ishmaelites: deceiving some with words, and holding the sword up against those who did not readily obey him, and forcing them to submit to him.

what_it_says: After the wife's death, Muhammad made himself chief, teacher and lawgiver of the Ishmaelites, deceiving some with words and forcing others with the sword.
context: Continuation of the same narrative (Book XIV ch. 17): after the wife's death Muhammad becomes leader and then conquers Syria and Byzantine provinces. Zonaras writes in the first half of the 12th century, as an epitomator.
limits: Describes the sword as a historical means of coercion in an account of Muhammad's rise; it is included under S as an account of how Islam spread, not as a call to violence. It is the author's narrative, not a quotation of Islamic sources; 'νομοθέτης' records the Byzantine view of Muhammad as a lawgiver, not any Qur'an text.
stance: own view (the author's narrative); not a quote from an opponent

quote_orig: τότε καὶ ὁ ψευδοπροφήτης Μωάμεθ ἐφάνη. οἱ γὰρ Ἰσμαηλῖται μέχρις Ἡρακλείου εἰδωλολάτρουν, τὴν Ἀστάρτην ἤγουν τὴν σελήνην προσκυνοῦντες· ἣν καὶ Χαβὲρ ὠνόμαζον, τοῦτ᾽ ἔστι μεγάλην. τηνικαῦτα δὲ ἀνέστη αὐτοῖς Μωάμεθ. οὗτος θητεύων γυναικί τινι πλουσίᾳ ὕστερον ἔλαβεν αὐτὴν εἰς γυναῖκα. εἶχε δὲ καὶ ἐπιληψίαν, καὶ θέλων κρύπτειν τὸ πάθος ἔλεγε τὸν Γαβριὴλ ὁρᾶν ἄγγελον καὶ μὴ φέρων αὐτοῦ τὴν θέαν ὀλιγωρεῖν καὶ πίπτειν. ἀξιόπιστα δὲ τὰ κατ᾽ αὐτὸν ἔδοξεν ἀπὸ μοναχοῦ τινὸς Ἀρειανοῦ ψευδομαρτυροῦντος αὐτῷ δι᾽ αἰσχροκέρδειαν.
own_translation_en: Then also the false prophet Muhammad appeared. For the Ishmaelites up to Heraclius were worshipping idols, adoring Astarte, that is the moon, whom they also called Chabera, that is, 'the great one'. At that time Muhammad arose for them. Serving a certain rich woman, he later took her as his wife. He had epilepsy, and, wishing to hide the affliction, he said that he saw the angel Gabriel, and that, since he could not bear the sight of him, he grew faint and fell down. What was said about him seemed credible from an Arian monk who gave false testimony for him for shameful gain.
quote_latin: ravit. tunc et falsus ille vates Moamethus exstitit. nam Ismaelitae ad Heraclium usque simulacra colebant, Astarten (quae luna est) adorantes; quam et Chaberam nuncupabant, hoc est magnam. hoc vero tempore Moamethus apud ipsos exortus est, qui cum apud divitem quamdam mulierem serviret, tandem eam uxorem accepit. laborabat is forte comitiali morbo, quem uti tegeret, angelum se Gabrielem conspicere dictitabat; cuius aspectum quia tolerare nequiret, fieri ut animo deiecto collaberetur. ea res fidem mereri visa fuit propter monachum quendam Arianum, qui lucri sui causa falsum ei testimonium perhibebat.
licence_note: Public domain Bonn 1836 edition; Latin printed beside the Greek; both read in the page image. The Latin 'ravit.' is the second half of 'imperavit' split by the page break.

what_it_says: Glykas calls Muhammad a false prophet who appeared after Heraclius and was epileptic, claiming that Gabriel appeared to him; the story seemed credible only on the word of an Arian monk who gave false witness for gain.
context: Annales, Pars IV, in the account of Constans II (reign after Heraclius), in the Bonn edition of 1836. Glykas places Muhammad after the Byzantine and Persian wars and before the Islamic doctrine summary that follows (passage 2). The reign and the sentence are in the author's own narration, not in a letter or a dialogue.
limits: Historical polemic: the 'false prophet' label is the author's; the moral attack on the Arian monk is a personal claim with no source named. The account of Ishmaelites as idolaters before Heraclius and the 'Chabera' name are not doctrinal polemic and are not checked against other sources. The Greek word 'ἠράνικε' of the following line is printed in a worn type and is discussed in passage 2. Translation is mine.
stance: own view (author's narration); the 'Arian monk' is a source named only as an inference

quote_orig: οὗτος ὁ Μωάμεθ εἰς Παλαιστίνην ἐλθὼν καὶ ἐντυχὼν Ἰουδαίοις, Ἀρειανοῖς, πρὸς δὲ καὶ Νεστοριανοῖς, ἀπὸ πάντων ἠράνικε, καὶ θρησκείαν ἰδίαν παρέδωκεν. οὐ παντάπασι δὲ χρῶνται τῷ νόμῳ· περιτομὴν γὰρ ἐδίδαξεν, οὐ μὴν δὲ καὶ σαββατίζειν. λέγει δὲ καὶ ἑαυτὸν κλειδοῦχον εἶναι τοῦ παραδείσου, τρεῖς δὲ ποταμοὺς φέρεσθαι ἐν αὐτῷ, μέλιτος οἴνου καὶ γάλακτος. λέγει καὶ αὐτὴν σκιὰν τοῦ Χριστοῦ σταυρωθῆναι διὰ φθόνον παρὰ τῶν Ἰουδαίων· αὐτὸν γὰρ ἀνελάβετο διὰ τὸ φιλεῖν ὁ θεός. οὗ καὶ εἰπόντος „σὺ ὁ Ἰησοῦς ἔλεγες ἑαυτὸν θεὸν” ἀπεκρίνατο ὡς οὐχ αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ὠνόμασε θεὸν ἀλλ᾽ οἱ ἄνθρωποι. ἐδίδαξε δὲ τὰ πάντα ὡρισμένα καὶ ἀπὸ θεοῦ γενέσθαι τοῖς ἀνθρώποις.
own_translation_en: This Muhammad, having gone to Palestine and met Jews, Arians and also Nestorians, gathered (something) from all of them and handed down a religion of his own. They do not use the law at all: he taught circumcision, but not the keeping of the Sabbath. He also says that he is the keeper of the keys of paradise, and that three rivers flow in it, of honey, wine and milk. He also says that the shadow of Christ itself was crucified through the envy of the Jews, since God had taken him up because he loved him. When someone said to him, 'You, Jesus, used to say that you are God', he replied that he did not himself call himself God, but men did. He taught that all things are determined and come from God for men.
quote_latin: idem Moamethus in Palaestinam profectus cum in Iudaeos Arianos et Nestorianos incidisset, quasi collectam quandam ab omnibus congessit, peculiaremque religionem suis tradidit. lege per omnia non utitur. circumcisionem retinendam tradit, sabbati observatione sublata. paradisi se clavigerum esse iactitat, in quo tres sint amnes, melle vino lacte fluentes. adserit umbram Christi tantum a Iudaeis per invidiam crucifixam esse, cum Christum ipsum deus ad se receperit, uti quem diligeret. rogatum id temporis Iesum a deo ipsene deum sese nuncupasset, respondisse nequaquam id se nominis usurpasse, verum homines illud sibi tribuisse. docet etiam sic evenire cuncta mortalibus ut definita sint divinitus.
licence_note: Public domain Bonn 1836 edition; Latin printed beside the Greek on p. 514 (read in the page image).

ἀπεκρίνατο ὡς οὐχ αὐτὸς ἑαυτὸν ὠνόμασε θεὸν
what_it_says: Glykas summarises what Muhammad taught: a religion gathered from Jews, Arians and Nestorians, circumcision without the Sabbath, paradise with milk, wine and honey rivers, the crucifixion of Christ's shadow, and a denial that Jesus called himself God.
context: The summary of Muhammad's doctrine follows his origin story on the same page (passage 1). Glykas presents these as claims that 'he says' (λέγει), in the register of a chronicler reporting a heresy rather than a systematic refutation.
limits: Glykas' summary is not a Qur'anic citation: the points (shadow of Christ, denial of Christ's divinity, paradise rivers) are reported without a quotation of the Qur'an or of an Islamic source. The word 'ἠράνικε' is printed in a worn type; my reading follows the image and matches the sense of the Latin 'collectam ... congessit' ('gathered'); the Bonn apparatus lists the variant ἐρρανίσατο (cod. F) for this word. The Latin is printed beside the Greek and is my own check, not an independent translation.
stance: reporting (Glykas reports Muhammad's claims with 'he says'; no opponent is quoted)

quote_orig: ἐξηγουμένους δὲ θεοφιλῶς τὸ εἰς σκάνδαλον δῆθεν κείμενον καὶ πρόσκομμα, καὶ διασαφοῦντας μὴ ὅλως Θεὸν οὐρανοῦ καὶ γῆς ποιητὴν καθυποβάλλεσθαι ἀναθέματι ἀλλὰ τὸν παρὰ τῷ λήρῳ καὶ δαιμονιώδει Μωάμετ ἀναπλαττόμενον ὁλόσφυρον Θεὸν καὶ μήτε γεννηθέντα μήτε γεννήσαντα (παρὰ Χριστιανοῖς μὲν γὰρ δοξάζεσθαι πατέρα Θεόν, αὐτὰ δὲ τὰ ἀπόβλητα τοῦ Μωάμετ ληρήματα τοῦτο ἀπαγορεύειν ὅλως· καὶ ἄλλως δὲ μὴ συνιέναι ἀκριβῶς ὁποῖόν τί ἐστι τὸ ὁλόσφυρον).
own_translation_en: Interpreting pious-wise the thing which was supposedly placed as a stumbling-block and an offence, and explaining that God, the maker of heaven and earth, should by no means be put under an anathema, but rather that god 'holosphyros', who is fashioned by the nonsense and demonic (Muhammad) and neither begotten nor begetting (for among Christians God is worshipped as Father, but the rejected nonsenses of Muhammad forbid this altogether; and moreover I do not clearly understand what the holosphyros is).
quote_latin: nec enim deum caeli et terrae conditorem ullo modo anathemate notari, sed holosphyrum illum deum, quem delirus et furiosus Machometus nec genitum nec gignentem confingeret: nam apud Christianos deum patrem celebrari, quod detestandis Machometi nugamentis plane prohibeatur. deinde se non satis intelligere quid sit illud holosphyrum

αὐτὰ δὲ τὰ ἀπόβλητα τοῦ Μωάμετ ληρήματα
what_it_says: Choniates has the court theologians say that the anathema must not fall on the creator God but on the 'holosphyros' god fashioned by the nonsensical and demonic Muhammad, who neither begets nor is begotten; he calls Muhammad's statements rejected nonsense, and says Christians confess God the Father.
context: In Book VII (Manuel I), the chapter where Choniates reports Manuel's last-years decree on the anathema in the catechetical tablet (p. 278). The subject of the sentence is the man who put the question to the clergy, here Manuel's court; the 'great Theodosios' is the Patriarch whom he summoned (Patriarch Theodosios; identification from a secondary search result, not verified in the primary text).
limits: Choniates' own polemical voice (not a neutral report): the terms 'nonsense', 'demonic' and 'holosphyros' are his. The Qur'anic formula (neither begets nor is begotten, cf. Qur'an 112) is paraphrased, not quoted, and Choniates explicitly says he does not understand what 'holosphyros' means. The Latin 'ad piam' in the preceding line is read from the image with some uncertainty. My English is literal and not a published translation.
stance: own view (Choniates' voice, narrating the decree and the clerics' objections)

quote_orig: Οἷον δὲ καὶ τόδ᾽ ἔρεξεν ἀνὴρ οὗτοσὶ περὶ τὸ πέρας τῆς αὐτοῦ βιοτῆς. ἐγκεῖται τῷ κατηχητικῷ πυκτίῳ μεθ᾽ ἑτέρων ἀφορισμῶν καὶ τὸ ἀνάθεμα τῷ Θεῷ τοῦ Μωάμετ, περὶ οὗ λέγει „οὔτε ἐγέννησεν οὔτε ἐγεννήθη,” καὶ ὅτι ὁλόσφυρός ἐστι. τὸν τοιοῦτον τοίνυν ἀναθεματισμὸν ἀπαλεῖψαι τῶν ὅλων κατηχητηρίων βίβλων προέθετο, ἀπ᾽ αὐτῆς τῆς ἐν τῇ μεγάλῃ ἐκκλησίᾳ πυκτίδος ἀρξάμενος. καὶ ἡ πρόφασις ὡς μάλα εὐπρόσωπος· ἔφασκε γὰρ ὡς εἰς σκάνδαλον πρόκειται τῶν μεταθεμένων Ἀγαρηνῶν εἰς τὴν καθ᾽ ἡμᾶς θεοσεβῆ πίστιν
own_translation_en: Of the same kind is what this man did near the end of his life. In the catechetical tablet he placed, along with other anathemas, the anathema against the god of Muhammad, about whom he says, 'neither did he beget nor was he begotten', and that he is holosphyros. Such an anathema he then resolved to erase from all catechetical books, beginning with the tablet in the Great Church. And the pretext was very plausible: he said that it was a stumbling-block placed in the way of Agarenes who were converting to our god-fearing faith.
quote_latin: Eiusdem generis illud etiam est quod Manuel sub vitae finem fecit. extat inter caeteras catecheticas tabulae sanctiones anathema in Machometi deum, quem nec genuisse nec genitum sed holosphyron esse affirmat. id anathema ex omnibus catecheticis libellis aboleri voluit ab ipsa magnae ecclesiae tabula auspicatus, idque ratione probabili suffultus, aiebat enim blasphemiis in deum qualibus

context: Choniates' report of Manuel I's last years (Book VII), just before the clergy's protest in the next page (passage 1). The 'man' is Manuel; the 'Agarenes' are Muslims whom the emperor wanted to attract.

stance: reporting (Choniates reports the emperor's act in his own voice; the emperor's defence is not quoted)

quote_orig: τὸν παρὰ τῷ Μωάμετ ὁλόσφυρον καὶ μὴ γεγεννημένον ἢ γεννήσαντα θεόν, πέρας εἰληφέναι πάντες τὴν προθέσπισιν ἔφασκον, ἐπεὶ καὶ μανίαν ἀτεχνῶς ὀρθὴν τε καὶ χειρίστην τὴν δόξαν εἶναι ταύτην ὡς τῆς ἀληθείας ἐπίπαν ἀντίθετον.
own_translation_en: That holosphyros god of Muhammad, who was neither begotten nor begetting: all said that the prophecy had reached its end, since this opinion is simply a right and worst madness, in general opposed to the truth.
quote_latin: verum esse deum, qui nec genitus esset nec genuisset, omnes id oraculum eo retulerunt, quod illa opinio a veritate alienissima germana et pessima esset insania.
licence_note: Public domain Bonn 1835; Latin printed on p. 286 below the Greek (read from the image).
keys: ὁλόσφυρον καὶ μὴ γεγεννημένον
ἔφασκον, ἐπεὶ καὶ μανίαν ἀτεχνῶς
ὡς τῆς ἀληθείας ἐπίπαν ἀντίθετον
what_it_says: Choniates reports that the courtiers interpreted the emperor's illness (and his death in September 1180) as the fulfilment of a prophecy: the opinion favouring Muhammad's God is, he says, a right and worst madness, opposed to the truth.
context: Manuel's last illness, in the Bonn text p. 286 (the emperor died in September, after a spring in which 'the dogma' had been raised in the question). The Latin says Manuel had been 'morbo correptus' in March and the dogma question was 'sopitum' by May; this matches the chronology (death 1180).
limits: Choniates' moralizing account of a court interpretation: the 'prophecy' is reported, not verified; it is the chronicler's judgement that the opinion is madness. The Latin wording 'omnes id oraculum eo retulerunt' is the translator's. Translation my own.
stance: own view (Choniates' narrative judgement; the courtiers' interpretation is reported)

ref: Laonici Chalcocondylae Historiarum libri decem, Bonn 1843, Liber III, p. 121 lines 1-11 (the Greek beginning 'Ὁ μέντοι νομοθέτης τούτων'; the top line of p. 121 names 'Μεχμέτης ὁ νομοθέτης').
url: https://archive.org/download/laonicichalcoco00bekkgoog/laonicichalcoco00bekkgoog.pdf (PDF p. 136 = printed p. 121; read as image at 200 dpi)
quote_orig: Ὁ μέντοι νομοθέτης τούτων ὁ Μεχμέτης παῖς λέγεται γενέσθαι Ἀλίεω, ἀπὸ Ἀραβίας τῆς εὐδαίμονος. ἐκθέμενον δὲ τὴν νομοθεσίαν αὐτοῦ ἀρχὴν μέντοι μηδὲν βιάζεσθαι, ἀναπείσαντά τε τοὺς Ἄραβας καὶ Σύρους μετὰ ταῦτα· μετὰ δὲ ταῦτα προσλαβόμενον τοῦ Ἀλίεω δυνάστου τε τῆς χώρας καὶ ἐπιτηδείου αὐτῷ, ὡς μάλιστα ἐπιόντα, προσάγεσθαι αὐτῷ εἰς τὴν νομοθεσίαν, ὅποι ἂν ἐπίῃ, τοὺς τὴν χώραν οἰκοῦντας.
own_translation_en: But the lawgiver of these people, Mechmetes, is said to have been the son of Ali, from happy Arabia. At the start of his lawgiving he used no force at all, but first won over the Arabs and then the Syrians by persuasion. Afterwards, taking into his company Ali, the lord of the region and his close friend, who was most present to him, he brought over to his lawgiving, wherever he went, the inhabitants of that land.
quote_latin: Aiunt legislatorem Mechmetem fuisse filium Haliis, Arabiam felicem incolentis. initio legislationis suae nihil vi egit, sed persuasione primum Arabes, deinde Syros cepit. postea in suam sententiam traduxit Haliem regionis administratorem, qui cum ipsi foret intima familiaritate coniunctus, facile omnes terrae suae incolas Mechmetis leges suscipere coegit.
licence_note: Public domain Bekker 1843; Latin printed beside the Greek on p. 121 (read from the image).
keys: ὁ Μεχμέτης παῖς λέγεται γενέσθαι Ἀλίεω
ἀναπείσαντά τε τοὺς Ἄραβας καὶ Σύρους
ἐκθέμενον δὲ τὴν νομοθεσίαν αὐτοῦ ἀρχὴν μέντοι μηδὲν βιάζεσθαι
what_it_says: Chalkokondyles reports that Muhammad (called Mechmetes, lawgiver) was said to be the son of Ali from Arabia; he began by persuasion, not force, winning Arabs and Syrians first, and only later pressed neighbours into his law with the help of a local lord.
context: Book III of the Histories, the Turkish digression on the origin of their religion and law (p. 120-121), reported by Chalkokondyles from accounts of the Turks; the Latin begins 'Aiunt' (they say).
limits: Reported origin story ('λέγεται', 'it is said'), not Chalkokondyles' own verdict; the name 'Mechmetes' and the Ali link are the Turkish-side tradition as he presents it. The Latin 'nihil vi egit' matches the Greek. My English is literal.
stance: reporting (Chalkokondyles reports what 'they say' about the lawgiver)

ref: Laonici Chalcocondylae Historiarum libri decem, Bonn 1843, Liber III, p. 126 lines 5-14 (Greek; the Latin beside it at the foot of the page).
url: https://archive.org/download/laonicichalcoco00bekkgoog/laonicichalcoco00bekkgoog.pdf (PDF p. 141 = printed p. 126; read as image at 200 dpi)
quote_orig: λέγεται δὲ τὸ σῆμα τοῦτο ὑπὸ λίθων πολυτελεστάτων κατασκευασθῆναι, καὶ ἐν μέσῳ τοῦ ναοῦ τὸ σῆμα μετεωριζόμενον ἀπαιωρεῖσθαι. ὅπερ ἀπίθανόν μοι δοκεῖ. διέχει δὲ ἀπὸ τοῦ χώρου τούτου, ἐν ᾧ τὸ σῆμα αὐτοῦ, ἐπὶ τοὺς ὡσεὶ σταδίους ἐνενήκοντα, καὶ ἐξιόντες ἐντεῦθεν ἵστανται ἐπὶ τὸν χῶρον τοῦτον. τοὺς τε νόμους αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ Ἀλκωρὰ ἐκτέθειται, τῇ τε ἀθανασίᾳ τιθέμενοι τῆς ψυχῆς. ἀγνωμοσύνης οὐδέν τι πάνυ οἴονται μετεῖναι τῷ θείῳ.
own_translation_en: It is said that this tomb was built of most precious stones, and that the tomb hangs suspended in the middle of the temple. That seems to me incredible. The place where his tomb is lies about ninety stades from this place, and those who come out from here go to that place. There they set out his laws and the Alkoran, and they hold that the soul is immortal. They think there is no ignorance at all in the divine.
quote_latin: sepulcrum eius compertum habeo extructum esse ex lapidibus pretiosissimis, et sublime pendere in medio templo. intervallum autem eius loci ubi sepulcrum conspicitur, usque ad hunc locum stadia continet circiter nonaginta. inde egressi ad eum locum contendunt, ibi siquidem leges et Alcorae explicantur. animae quoque immortalitatem astruunt. nec numini ignorantiam ascribunt.
licence_note: Public domain Bekker 1843; Latin printed beside the Greek on p. 126 (read from the image). Note: the Latin does not render 'ὅπερ ἀπίθανόν μοι δοκεῖ' (which seems incredible to me).
keys: ἀπαιωρεῖσθαι. ὅπερ ἀπίθανόν μοι δοκεῖ
τοὺς τε νόμους αὐτοῦ καὶ τὰ Ἀλκωρὰ ἐκτέθειται
τῇ τε ἀθανασίᾳ τιθέμενοι τῆς ψυχῆς
what_it_says: Chalkokondyles reports a Muslim pilgrimage to the tomb of Mechmetes, the supposed suspended tomb, and says it seems incredible to him; he notes that the pilgrims there explain the laws and the Alkoran and hold that the soul is immortal.
context: Continuation of the Turkish religion digression in Book III (p. 126), immediately after the description of the pilgrimage route and the tomb legend; he then returns to the story of Temir (Timur).
limits: Chalkokondyles reports pilgrims' practice; the marvel of the suspended tomb he calls implausible, and the Latin omits that judgement. 'Alkoran' is his word for the Qur'an; no Qur'anic text is quoted. My English is literal. The sentence 'ἀγνωμοσύνης ... μετεῖναι' is read from the image; a slight OCR doubt remains in the verb ἵστανται (image reads ἵστανται).
stance: reporting (Chalkokondyles reports, and expresses scepticism only about the tomb legend)

ref: Nicephori Gregorae Byzantina historia, Bonn (CSHB) 1829–1855, p. 228 lines 13-18 (Greek; the Latin printed beside it on p. 228).
url: https://archive.org/download/nicephorigregor07schogoog/nicephorigregor07schogoog.pdf (PDF p. 253 = printed p. 228; read as image at 200 dpi)
quote_orig: τὸ γε μὴν θεῖον τοῦ Χριστοῦ εὐαγγέλιον μετὰ τοῦ Δαυϊτικοῦ ψαλτήρος αἰδοῖ πολλῇ τοὺς οἰκείους τηρεῖν ἐνετέλλετο· εἰώθεσαν γὰρ καὶ Ἰσμαηλῖται τιμᾶν προφήτας τε ἅπαντας καὶ ἅμα τὸν σωτῆρα Χριστὸν ὡς ἕνα τῶν προφητῶν.
own_translation_en: He ordered that the divine Gospel of Christ, together with the Psalter of David, be kept with great reverence by his people, for the Ishmaelites were accustomed both to honour all the prophets and, at the same time, Christ the Saviour as one of the prophets.
quote_latin: soliti erant etiam Ismaelitae colere quum omnes prophetas tum etiam Christum redemtorem, quippe qui esset unus e prophetis.
licence_note: Public domain Bonn CSHB (1829–1855) on archive.org; Latin printed beside the Greek on p. 228 (read from the image).
keys: εἰώθεσαν γὰρ καὶ Ἰσμαηλῖται τιμᾶν προφήτας τε ἅπαντας
ὡς ἕνα τῶν προφητῶν
soliti erant etiam Ismaelitae colere
what_it_says: Gregoras notes that the Ishmaelites (Turks) honour all the prophets and also Christ the Saviour as one of the prophets, a summary of the Muslim view of Jesus as a prophet.
context: Gregoras' narrative of Gregory Palamas' captivity among the Turks (1354-55): a Turkish captor mocks Palamas, goes through his books, and throws some into the sea, but a Gospel and the Psalter are kept with respect. The remark explains why the Turks spared those books.
limits: Gregoras is an enemy of Palamas and writes this to show Palamas' treatment and the Turks' attitude; the statement about the Ishmaelites is a general remark, not a Qur'anic quotation. The Latin is the Bonn translation (translator not verified). Translation my own.
stance: reporting (Gregoras reports Turkish practice in his own narrative voice)
